rv.q: Vietgone is easily the freshest, most exuberantly youthful piece I’ve seen at MTC in ages: a punch-drunk mash-up of hip-hop, road movies, sex farce and Vietnamese-American history.
It is overtly rollicking and sneakily moving.
The playful meta-theatricality of the piece, a co-production of MTC and South Coast Repertory in Costa Mesa, Calif., is indicated early on.

The laughter subsides; the play’s flaws recede; and we are left with a resonantly ambiguous picture of the manner in which wars, and the tides of refugees they often result in, have an indelible impact on individual lives.
Nguyen, who came out of the downtown geek culture celebrated by this troupe Vampire Cowboys, shows here that he's also comfortable working in more traditional theatrical forms.

Beautifully conveyed through director May Adrales' unapologetically theatrical staging, Vietgone makes you believe that epic tales of heroism and loss exist all around us in this nation of immigrants.

"A high-octane, swiftly hysterical, well-crafted experience. A mash-up of rap, hip-hop, and characters that never say die, it is a super-smart, irresistible way to talk about war...But it’s not a musical–it’s a play and an experience, and originally theatrical.
“Vietgone” is comic and compassionate; overlong (by at least 15 minutes) — and overdue.
The result of his loving meddling is an evening that may not visit a lot of new territory, but goes in all the familiar places in alternately refreshing, funny, and moving ways.

The springiness in the script is enhanced by May Adrales's vivid staging, which features confessional rap interludes, a hallucinatory fight sequence, and graphic-novel-like projections designed by Jared Mezzocchi.
Vietgone is a certified original -- sometimes to a fault.

Part playful, part dead serious, Qui Nguyen, born in America to two Vietnamese refugee parents, takes dead aim at both Baby Boomers and Millennials alike in his innovative new work and hits both targets.

Downtown theatergoers know the work of Qui Nguyen from his productions at the Vampire Cowboy Theatre Company which he co-founded in 2000. While Vietgone is often untidy and overly complex, this exuberant autobiographical play is a fascinating look at the Vietnamese American experience from their point of view written by an insider.
The emotional elements do not consistently fuse with the production’s approach but it’s sexy, funny, and smart a lot of the time.
The problem with "Vietgone" is that its focus is scattered, often seeming to slide from the story to the novelty of its telling.
Vietgone, in fact, may be a perfect example of millennial narcism.
Vietgone is definitely not to miss, and highly deserving of many more successful productions in the future.
This is the doing of a highly skilled playwright.
Playwright Nguyen has developed characters with believable conflicts that drive an intriguing and transformative plot.
Nguyen’s Vietgone is about loss, while his characters use a brave determination to survive in a way that is hip, jarring and oh so watchable.
Vietgone moves into newer territory for the usually staid pieces seen at Manhattan Theatre Club...
It is often wildly entertaining, and yet the play provokes thought about the plight of those who left Vietnam during the infamous war.
"Vietgone" remains a poignant, touching, waggish and even awe-inspiring love-letter to America's global village.
'Vietgone' is a must-see...It has laughs, ninjas, a serious rap flow, and a rare perspective on the Vietnam War.
I found it refreshing and worthwhile.
A bit too zany at times (it was the '70s after all) and a bit too long and drawn out in others—this play has a future if tightened and given a general tune-up.

cn.t: Critics praise this inventive, high-energy play blending hip-hop, action, and humor to tell a Vietnamese refugee love story, though some find it uneven and overlong. The fresh approach and cultural commentary resonate despite occasional tonal wobbles.
